new_statements.rule_in_words: No statement about word stress exists for Geruma. The only description (Schuh 1978, 1.5 h of fieldwork) treats it as a two-tone language (H, L; occasional HL falls, word-final rises, downstep) and its 'Remarks on Phonology' section says only that nothing unusual was noted. The only stress statement is family-level: Schuh 2017 (A Chadic Cornucopia, ch. 1 p. 6 and ch. 5 p. 89) says no Chadic language has stress as a prosodic parameter; prosodic prominence is a function of tone, syllable weight and intonation.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Schuh 1978 p. 125-126 notes that in his 21-verb sample monosyllabic and CVC- verbs are high-toned and CVVC- verbs low-toned, i.e. verb tone is partly predictable from shape, but he cannot exclude a lexical tone distinction in verbs.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (citation forms and perfective paradigms); tone statements on p. 9 are for the whole group (Bole, Bele, Kirfi, Galambu, Gera, Geruma as recorded by Schuh), the fn. 1 statement is Geruma-specific. Schuh 2017's 'no stress' is a family-level (Chadic) statement, not based on Geruma data.
new_statements.identity_note: Schuh 1978 describes the Duurum variety (Glottolog dialect duur1238; village Duurum on the Ningi road, the eastern-most Geruma village), supplemented by Shimizu's notes from Sum (summ1239); Schuh notes that Sum speech differs from Duurum (e.g. negative suffix with final nasal, glottonym Gyeermu vs Geerum). Grambank codes geru1240 from Schuh 1978 + Zoch 2014. No source describes the Gamsawa/Gamshi variety (gams1239).

sources.note: The only first-hand description (1.5 h at Duurum, 16 Apr 1975, plus Shimizu's 1974 Sum notes and Gowers 1907). Geruma sec. 2 'Remarks on Phonology' (p. 122) is one line: 'no unusual features were noted'. Footnote 1 p. 133: 'Since I am sure that Geruma has only two phonemic tones..'; group-level Introduction p. 9: 'These languages all have two phonemic tones only', with falls, word-final rises and downstep. Verb tone classes sec. 7.1.2 pp. 125-126. Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the book (0 hits in the text layer; Geruma pages read as images).

sources.note: FAMILY-LEVEL only; Geruma appears just in the Bole-Tangale classification list. Ch. 1 p. 6 (book outline): '- stress: no Chadic language has stress as a prosodic parameter'. Ch. 5 'Tone' p. 89: 'All Chadic languages are tone languages.. Stress as distinctive prosodic property has been discussed in Hunter (1980) for Hausa and Wolff (1983, 2015b) for Lamang.., but prosodic amplitude in Chadic phonological systems generally is a function of the interaction of tone, syllable weight, and intonation and plays no role that is not attributable to those properties.'
